description.en-US: The business identifier quoted to the ordering system and to support: a 4-character source code, a 3-character method code and the order code. It is generated, never supplied, so that its three parts always agree with the record they describe.

The identifier the gateway knows this order by, and the key every callback arrives under. Distinct from order_id because the gateways limit what they will carry, and because a callback must be matched without parsing anything out of it.
Which system asked for the payment. The default names the vending machines, which were the only caller of the service this module supersedes.

System-managed lifecycle state. Immutable to clients: it is advanced only by create_payment, by refund, by a gateway callback and by the watchdog, because a status set by hand would claim money moved that nothing moved.

Amount to collect, in the order's currency. Decimal rather than an integer count of minor units, because how many minor units a currency has is a property of the currency: storing amounts that way would push a per-currency scale into everything that reads one.
How much of amount has been given back. System-managed by the refund action, which is also what keeps it from exceeding amount.

The currency this order is denominated in. A reference into Essential's currency master, held as a plain id rather than an edge: the currency belongs to another module, and a foreign key across that boundary would make this module's schema depend on Essential's table. Its code, symbol and decimal places all stay in Essential.

How the payer pays. A reference to a configured method rather than an enum value, so that offering a gateway under a second merchant account, or withdrawing one, is a data change rather than a release.
What the payer sees the payment described as.
Where the ordering system is notified once the payment settles. Held per order rather than configured, because one deployment serves several ordering systems.
How the most recent attempt to notify return_url ended. A failure is what the retry job looks for.
History of the notification attempts, as {"entries": [{status, type, timestamp}]}. Wrapped in an object because this type has no array form. It is what stops the retry job re-notifying forever.

Everything about this order that is specific to the method paying it: the inputs the adapter required at create time — a terminal id for a card terminal, nothing at all for a wallet — alongside the gateway's own create and refund responses, kept verbatim as the evidence when a payment is disputed.

This is a map rather than a column per method because the set of methods is data: a column named for one gateway's needs would be dead weight on every order paid another way, and adding a gateway would mean a migration. Each adapter declares which keys it requires and validates its own, so no code outside the adapter knows what a given method needs.
